title: KALANYOS AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
summary: In Kalanyos and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Sandor Kalanyos, Tamas Kalanyos, and Istvan Rozsa—are Romanian nationals of Roma origin, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre. The case highlights the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to racially motivated violence and the failure of state authorities to protect them or provide justice. In June 1991, following a dispute in the hamlet of Plăieşii de Sus, Harghita County, tensions escalated after a non-Roma night-watchman insulted Roma individuals, leading to a fight and subsequent police detention of the first applicant. In retaliation, non-Roma villagers assaulted two Roma men, resulting in the death of Adam Kalanyos, the uncle of two applicants. Shortly after, a public threat was posted warning that Roma homes would be burned. Despite being informed, local authorities failed to intervene and instead advised the Roma to flee. On 9 June 1991, non-Roma villagers destroyed all twenty-eight Roma houses by arson, forcing the applicants and their families to live in stables under inhumane conditions for a year, without compensation for their losses. Investigations by Romanian authorities were inadequate, marked by ethnic bias and eventual closure due to prescription periods, with officials blaming the victims. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found the application partly inadmissible. This case remains significant as it exposes the persistent impunity for anti-Roma violence in post-communist Europe and the systemic barriers Roma and Travellers face in accessing justice.
